pars.text: In an Aristotelian context the regular English translation of the Greek σοφία is 'wisdom'. But as is well enough known, σοφία originally meant skill or cleverness in the arts and handicrafts. Early instances apply it to carpentry, medicine, poetry and the like.[406] In Xenophon (Anab I.2.8), immediately before Aristotle's time, it is still used unhesitatingly for ability in music. On reaching the river Marsyas, Xenophon recalled the legend of the contest between the satyr Marsyas and Apollo. It was a contest περί σοφίας, with σοφία understood as proficience in flute-playing. The satyr lost, and as a penalty was flayed alive. Aristotle himself was well aware of this use of the term 'wisdom' to denote excellence in artistic work, as with Phidias in stone and Polyclitus in bronze (EN VI.7, 1141a9-12). He felt no incongruity in saying that professional craftsmen were held to be 'wiser' than amateurs (Metaph I.1, 981a25; b11).

Nevertheless in making those statements the Stagirite was aiming to show that wisdom has to be the most perfect kind of knowledge. It should be something far above sense cognition, something that gives the ultimate reasons for things, something eminently teachable and free, something more divine than human, something theoretical rather than practical (Metaph I.1-2, 980a21 ff.). One might ask what caused this shift in meaning from the primitive and much more modest sense of the term. Aristotle gives his own answer. He develops his rationale for the exaltation of σοφία to such a high peak. His reasons are profound and enduring. They will be the object of the present discussion. But first a glance at the background against which these reasons emerged is in order.

Already with Heraclitus (DK fr. 41) the notion of the wise (το σοφόν) was centered on the way the whole universe is directed: 'What is wise is one thing, to understand rightly how all things are steered through all'. The notion bore expressly on the all-pervading unity of things (fr. 50). Further, 'Wisdom is to speak the truth and to act according to nature, with understanding' (fr. 112). The broadest sweep of all is accorded to wisdom in these fragments. It is given the most exalted place in knowledge. But there is no restriction of it to the theoretical sphere. Rather, it is meant to bear upon what is being done. It is aimed at regulating human conduct. The scorn of Heraclitus (fr. 40) for the polymathy he saw in Pythagoras and others seems to indicate sharply the practical cast in which he projected the highest kind of knowledge.

Yet it is in fact to Pythagoras, whom Heraclitus had characterized as a polymath, that legend attributes the raising of wisdom to a divine and purely theoretical status. Cicero (Tusc Disp 5.3.8), writing about the transition from the term σοφία to φιλοσοφία, repeated the story that Pythagoras claimed to be conversant with no art at all. Rather, he was a philosopher, a lover of σοφία. Here was a radical break with the term's primitive sense. The new meaning of σοφία was illustrated (5.3.9) by the motives of people going to the games. Some went to compete for prizes, others to sell wares, and still others to watch as spectators. The spectators in the sphere of knowledge as well as in sports, the legend insisted, enjoy the highest type of freedom. They are slaves neither to glory nor to money. The same illustration is recorded by Diogenes Laertius (8.8), with the purpose of showing that what the philosopher pursues is truth.

The legend about Pythagoras was quoted directly or indirectly from a fourth-century B.C. source, from which Diogenes Laertius (1.12) also cites the assertion of Pythagoras that no one but God is wise.[407] The legend accordingly reflects the mentality of the mid-fourth century to which Aristotle was exposed. It had raised the meaning of σοφία to a sphere regarded as above all the arts and crafts. The language and similes of the legend are echoed in the assertions about wisdom in the opening chapters of the Metaphysics. Circulating in the immediate background of Aristotle, it shows how the meaning of σοφία had been transferred from the humble proficiencies of the carpenter and the flute-player to a knowledge of reality as a whole, a knowledge that bore upon truth itself instead of upon a particular kind of object. It meant a supremely free knowledge that was theoretical in character and that was attributed in its fullness to the deity alone. Humans could but love it and strive after it. They could be only philosophers, friends or lovers of wisdom.

Again in the immediate background of Aristotle, Plato (Apol 21A) had the Delphic oracle declare that no man was wiser than Socrates. Socrates was described as going to the men who were reputed to be wise in public life, the πολιτικοί. He questioned them one by one, and saw that they did not know anything about the good or the καλόν. He concluded that he was wiser than they because he knew that he himself did not know anything about those lofty topics (21B). Translated into the terms of the Pythagorean legend, this would mean that Socrates knew the truth in a way that was missed by the political leaders of the city-state. The sweep was broad, all-inclusive. He could see that none of them was wise, and that wisdom is a divine prerogative. A human being could only strive after it, with the full realization that what was regarded by the public men as wise did not at all have the character of wisdom.

After the rounds of men in public life, Plato (Apol 22A-C) had Socrates go to the poets. He found they could not explain the many fine things they said in verse. This meant that their poetry did not proceed from wisdom (σοφία) but from some kind of inspiration they did not understand. Like prophets and oracles, they said things without knowing what was meant. Yet they thought they were the wisest in all other things as well.

Finally, and of most concern to our present point, Plato (Apol 22CE) had Socrates go to the artisans, the people who work with their hands. In what seems remarkable sensitivity to the primitive meaning of the Greek σοφία, Socrates knew that he would find in them genuine knowledge about many worthwhile things. He was not disappointed. In the things in which they were expert they were 'wiser' than he. But he also found that because of their success in technical matters, they thought they were wise to a supreme degree in the greatest of concerns. This foolishness of theirs, Socrates concluded, blotted out the wisdom they actually had. It left them victims of the same ludicrous mistake encountered among the poets, that skill in one art gave wisdom likewise about the highest things.

In these and other reflections of the Platonic Socrates, a surprisingly exact background may be observed for Aristotle's treatment of wisdom in the opening chapter of the Metaphysics. The artisans and the people who have experience are acknowledged to be wise in their own right, though with a lower degree of wisdom (Metaph I.1, 981b5; b31). Then the value of myth, and of the poetic intuition that wisdom is the privilege of the deity only, is recognized. However, the proviso is added that the poets are often wrong, and in particular are wrong in saying that the deity begrudges wisdom to men (I.2, 982b28-983a10). For Socrates, the poets did not know the reasons for the objects of their intuitions. Accordingly Aristotle, in the course of outlining his own conception of wisdom as knowledge through cause, can readily take the stand the poets need not always be trusted in what they have to say about wisdom. They did not deter Socrates from pursuing his quest. Why could they go wrong so easily? Aristotle's notion of wisdom would suggest the reason. They could go wrong because they lacked knowledge in terms of cause.

Noteworthy, though, is the shift from one extreme to the other in the notion of σοφία. Originally referring to specialized and plebeian proficiencies, it had now come to be used in elite Greek philosophical circles for an all-embracing kind of knowledge, a knowledge that was proper to the deity rather than to humans, a knowledge that was described as aloofly theoretical in the way spectators watched athletic events aside from any advantageous pursuit of fame or wealth. In Plato it can still have its ancient sense of the technical arts (Prot 321D). But in the way in which it is to be learned from Socrates' teaching (Symp 175C-E) it has as its object the fairest things of all (204B). Wisdom contemplates beauty in itself and in its entirety, divine beauty (211C-212A). Σοφία is still recognized as applicable to the arts and crafts, but on reaching the highest and divine levels it lets the particular types fade out of its vision, quite as Socrates in the Apology (22D) had the shortcomings of technicians' σοφία blot out or cover up any claim to be the wisdom he was seeking.

Viewed in the Socratic perspective, the wisdom of the men who professed to be wise turned out to be sham and pretense, wisdom in appearance only (Aristotle, Metaph IV.2, 1004B17; 26). Down through the centuries it carried the label of 'sophistry', the ironical designation to which the claim of its devotees left it open. In modern times, however, the notion 'sophisticated' came to designate the opposite of the naive or credulous or over-simple, with the sense of worldly-wise. Still more recently it has acquired the meaning of the highly technical, in application to giant computers and to weaponry like the exocets and the cruise missiles. The odyssey of the Greek term σοφία seems in its derivatives to have run a complete circle from lowly beginnings in the crafts to the far remote and exalted heights of contemplation, and then through the opposite pole of sham faςade and back to its primitive sense of skill in making gadgets, as seen in the modern high technology. Words have their magic.

Sidetracked in this odyssey of the Greek σοφία, however, is the meaning ordinarily given to the term 'wisdom' in English conversation, and in the way its equivalents have usually been understood in both European and eastern traditions. 'Wisdom', as regularly taken in English, bears first and foremost on practical conduct (OED, s.v.a). It means knowing how to do the right thing under the circumstances. A person is wise if he can estimate a situation correctly and make the proper decision in regard to action. In fact, people who are very theoretical are often found to be not so wise in what they do. It is wise, for instance, not to take the extra drink before driving. It is wise to avoid extremes in conduct, wise to profit by one's experience and the experience of others, wise to stay within the limits of one's own capacities. The wisdom looked for in statesmen is not profound theoretical philosophy, but rather the type of thinking that will guide public affairs to success. Metaphysicians are quite inconspicuous in modern governments and in the history of anglophone public affairs. The notion of the Platonic philosopher-king is given scant attention. To be wise, when the question about wisdom is asked in English, is primarily to be practical, to do things in the right way.

The English term 'wisdom' has in point of fact from the earliest traceable times signified the knowledge that brings about praiseworthy human action. It means the proper guiding of conduct. In the translations of the ancient biblical writings it referred to the ability of Solomon to make the correct decisions in governing and in administering justice, and to the maxims for conduct handed down in the books of Proverbs and Wisdom. Correspondingly in other cultures and traditions the prized heritage of what we express as their wisdom bore mostly upon the way they did things.[408] Greece was hardly an exception. Along with the application to the arts and crafts, the term σοφία became used extensively for the correct guidance of practical conduct (LSJ, s.v.2). Lawgivers like Solon were wise. Thales, too, was included among the seven wise men of Greece. But even though the doxographical tradition emphasized the speculative knowledge of Thales, the picture handed down by Diogenes Laertius (1.35-7) would suggest that he lived in popular esteem rather through his pithy maxims for moral guidance. The contemplation of the heavens, that caused him to fall into the well he could not see (1.34), needed to be balanced by the story of his shrewdness in getting a corner on the oil-presses in the year he knew there would be a bumper crop of olives, and thereby making a lot of money. Speculative knowledge had to be represented as something able to be put to good use. That seems to be what merited it the popular title of 'wisdom'.

Aristotle, nevertheless, consistently and deliberately excludes practical knowledge from the designation σοφία. He reports (EN, VI.7,1141b2-9) that people say men like Thales and Anaxagoras are wise, but are lacking in knowledge of what is to their own interests. The knowledge they do have is regarded as useless, because it is not a pursuit of human goods. Aristotle is thereby making an effort to show that the exclusion of practical knowledge from σοφία is in accord with popular opinion. For himself he expressly limits σοφία to the speculative field. To designate the traditionally recognized wisdom of the practical sphere, he uses in sharp contrast the Greek term φρόνησις. It is a word of difficult etymology, but it implied insight (see Frisk, s.v. φρόνις) and concern. It accordingly served Aristotle's purposes with neat satisfaction. But it does raise a problem for the English translator, as a little reflection will readily bring out.

The traditionally accepted Latin translation of φρόνησις is prudentia. This proved satisfactory enough as long as the meaning of the basic word from which prudentia was contracted, namely providentia, was kept in mind (as in 'prudentes possumus dicere, id est providentes' [Cicero, Div 1.49.111)). Providentia meant foresight, and presumed the notion of wisdom in the knowledge by which it provides for the future. The concept of divine providence, in which that term became currently used, could hardly be represented apart from the notion of the divine wisdom. But in modern languages that tend to emphasize the aspect of caution in their concept of prudence, the situation is different. The notion expressed by the Aristotelian φρόνησις is thereby greatly narrowed. Sometimes prudence may even be taken to imply a hindrance to correct moral action, instead of being its source, as in the complaint that a person is too prudent. On the whole, 'prudence' does not seem a satisfactory translation of the Aristotelian term, even though it is still widely used.[409]

The Oxford translation regularly uses the English phrase 'practical wisdom' for the Greek φρόνησις. This has the great advantage of retaining the notion of wisdom in the translation. But it requires the use of 'speculative wisdom' to render exactly what is in contrast meant by σοφία, and that may be awkward at times. A much lesser discord is that 'practical wisdom' just by itself seems to suggest the notion of 'worldly-wise', of attention to one's immediate interests instead of those that are more elevated and remote. But in Aristotle the term has to apply to the guidance of all moral action. 'Practical wisdom', nevertheless, renders more exactly the force of φρόνησις in meeting the ordinary English acceptation of wisdom. In this fundamental regard it is more satisfactory than 'prudence'.

These considerations emphasize the requirement of bringing the Aristotelian φρόνησις under the range of the English term 'wisdom'. Although Aristotle, against the alleged Pythagorean and Socratic background of eminence for speculative thought, could separate the notions of φρόνησις and σοφία, the English term 'wisdom' cannot be excluded from the guidance of practical life. In fact, as it is used alone in ordinary English speech it expresses forcefully enough what Aristotle meant by φρόνησις. To act correctly is to act wisely. A person of wisdom is one who knows what had best be done in each situation in daily life. That is the fundamental and outstanding sense of the term in everyday English speech. To focus it on purely speculative knowledge, in saying, for instance, that a great mathematician is wise on account of his mathematical knowledge, or that a metaphysician is wise in virtue of his proficience in his discipline, would hardly be an ordinary use of the English word 'wise'. Wisdom is first and foremost a type of knowledge that bears upon conduct. While Aristotle could report that people regarded Thales as having wisdom but not φρόνησις, in English their comment would be better expressed by saying that they considered Thales to be learned but not very wise.

As regards translation of Aristotle, however, there is no such easy solution. After all, σοφία is the Greek word for wisdom. 'Wisdom' has to be used as the literal translating term. Aristotle's artificial restriction on its use can be explained, but cannot change the translation. Even though in every instance the terms 'wisdom' and 'wise' may render correctly in English the Aristotelian φρόνησις and its adjectival forms, they have been preempted for theoretical knowledge by Aristotle's exclusion of φρόνησις from the range of σοφία. Intolerable confusion would result, for instance in having to say at 1141b3-5 that Anaxagoras and Thales were regarded as 'wise but not wise'. In consequence, translations like 'prudence' or 'practical wisdom' have to be retained for φρόνησις. 'Wisdom' can then be explained as restricted in Aristotle to speculative wisdom. This meaning of the English word 'wisdom' is legitimate and is recognized (OED s.v.2a) without hesitation in the sense of knowledge or erudition, especially when elevated or abstruse. Though translation by 'speculative wisdom' may not be acceptable, explanation of the Aristotelian term by that phrase is entirely in order and quite in accord with understandable English. While the use of 'wisdom' or 'wise' to designate expertness in the arts or crafts would have to be regarded as archaic, their application to speculative thinking is not.

In an answer to the question about the meaning of wisdom in Aristotle, then, φρόνησις or practical wisdom has to be included when the question is posed in English. Undoubtedly there is difficulty in both English and Greek in compressing the speculative knowledge and the practical knowledge under the same term. The root of the difficulty lies in the Aristotelian conception of the theoretical and the practical. The two have radically and irreducibly divergent origins. They proceed from different first principles, principles that are pertinently distinct in kind. The first principles of theoretical knowledge are found in the independently existent physical world, the world of reality. The principles of practical knowledge are found in human choice (Metaph E. 1, 1025b18-24). But the world in which men choose and act is the real world in which they exist and live. The world in which human conduct takes place is the same world that is viewed theoretically by the speculative sciences. Conduct is not separable from reality.

As a result, theoretical knowledge is required for wise action. One has to get information on the condition of the roads before making a wise decision about driving on a stormy night in winter. Intelligence is of the utmost importance for decisions made by generals in war. Aristotle requires considerable theoretical knowledge of the soul for moral philosophy (EN I.13, 1102a18-26), and makes use of it in determining the nature of true human happiness (I.7, 1097b28-1098a17). Yet the theoretical knowledge is not metamorphosed into practical knowledge. Its nature remains the same. But it is used by the practical wisdom as an instrument required for making the right decision. In fact, the difference between making the right and the wrong decision will often depend upon the knowledge available for the deliberation. Correct orientation of the appetitive side of the soul is basic, but it has to use theoretical knowledge as its instrument. The more complicated the situation, the greater will be the extent of the theoretical knowledge that is required.

What is meant in English by 'wisdom', then, will have to range in this way over both the practical and the theoretical areas. The two areas are included, proportionately to the circumstances. The difficulty arises if one attempts to reduce either of the two types to the other. This attempt at systematization in Aristotle is bound to fail. That has been imputed to him as a fault.[410] But the very nature of practical wisdom requires theoretical wisdom as its instrument. The two go together in the deliberation. They lend themselves, accordingly, to designation under the one global term 'wisdom', even though their respective functions have to be carefully kept distinct.

Against this combined historical and philosophical background the notion of wisdom outlined in the opening chapters of Aristotle's Metaphysics may now be approached. The first sentence, so well-known, bursts over the whole area like the sun emerging suddenly from a heavy cloud covering. By their very nature, it proclaims, all persons reach out in desire to know. They yearn for knowledge just in itself, regardless of whatever other advantages it may bring them. The point at issue is aptly illustrated by sense cognition. People love to see and to hear, and to perceive through their other senses, aside from any utility. Sight is the outstanding example, insofar as it most of all brings us to knowledge of things and makes clear their distinguishing traits. Even apart from anything we plan on doing, we prize the act of seeing, one might say, above all other kinds of sensation (Metaph I.1, 980a21-7).

The force of this illustration is readily felt. Sight brings out most clearly and most sharply the manifold variety of traits in things. We delight in viewing a beautiful landscape or a great painting. We contemplate it just for itself, for its own beauty. Aristotle emphasizes the conclusion that we may choose to do so just for the contemplation itself. There is no need to mention how useful sight is for other things. To walk around, to work, to associate with others, sight is of the greatest utility. Just the thought of a white cane will drive home that benefit poignantly. There is no denying the advantages of sight for everyday living. Aristotle's one point is that aside from these advantages, aside from all utility, we prize sight for its own sake.

The point merits attention. There has been a temptation to explain Aristotle's attitude towards theoretical philosophy as an outright denial of its usefulness. To the question 'What use is metaphysics?' the answer has been given, by way of shocking students into reaction, that metaphysics has no use. The soothing explanation is then proffered that it is above all use. Anything useful is inferior, because subordinated to something else, the end for which it is useful. Aristotle's metaphysics is immediately depicted as something meant just for itself, not subordinated to anything else, and accordingly above any utility. What is forgotten is that Aristotle uses metaphysics to present to practical reason the most choice-worthy goal of human conduct. He uses theoretical philosophy to provide the moralist with the requisite knowledge of the human soul, which helps him to outline and understand the virtues. Theoretical wisdom plays an important even though only instrumental role in the philosophy that guides human conduct. It has its use, even though it exercises its own profound attraction just for its own sake.

Illustrated by the example of sight, the notion of wisdom is rapidly developed by Aristotle in ascending scale in the first chapter of the Metaphysics. Upon sensation there follows memory, from memory and imagination there follows experience, and finally from experience there follow art and science in human life. The difference of procedure in this final stage is brought about by the grasp of the universal in experience. To know something universally is to know it according to the form by which it is seen to be like others, in the way in which for instance Socrates is like Callias and other men, and by which a fever in Socrates is recognized as the same disease as that from which Callias is suffering. Pressing the inquiry further, Aristotle shows that knowing something universally means knowing it in terms of its cause. The causal knowledge gives to art and science the preeminence over mere experience (Metaph I.1, 980a27-981a12).

The explanation of universality as knowledge through cause is not pursued any further for the moment. The notion seems difficult at first sight. 'Cause' today usually means what Aristotle called the efficient cause. Efficient causality is always exercised by something individual. A universal does not act or produce. Only the individual physician cures (981a18). Only an individual mason lays bricks. Only individual caterpillars cause damage to trees. In general, in Aristotle's metaphysics, no universal is a substance, and only substances are agents. How, then, does knowing the cause give rise to universal knowledge? In the line of efficient causality, one might trace the individual causes back indefinitely, without arriving at anything over and above that would explain universality.

Aristotle, however, writes as though this connection between universality and cause was quite obvious to his hearers. A Platonic background pointed to the Ideas or forms for the ultimate explanation of things, and the medical example and language just used by Aristotle would recall the technical medical term είδος by which diseases were classified.[411] The notion 'form' seemed to express the difference between haphazard and scientific knowledge, between mere experience and artistic or scientific training. So, in introducing the causes in the Metaphysics (I.3, 983a28), Aristotle observes parenthetically 'The question why is carried back ultimately to the λόγος, and the first reason why is a cause and first principle'. Form is spoken of as the first of the causes, and as the ultimate answer to the question why.[412] Form will be shown later in the Metaphysics (VII. 17, 1041a10 ff.; VIII.6, 1045b3-7) to be the cause of a thing's being of such and such a kind, and of its being a unit. The form is the cause of universality and of singularity in the thing. In the rout simile at the end of the Posterior Analytics (II.17, 100a17), in a context quite like that in the first chapter of the Metaphysics, Aristotle is able to say "The singular is perceived, but the perception is of the universal". The prospect of having to face an infinite series in searching out the cause of universality is forestalled in the most successful manner of avoiding the series, namely by showing that the first step does not have to be taken. The individual is what the universal expresses, not all individuals taken together, but each in turn. Each individual is 'severally', to use the felicitous Ross translation (Metaph V.26, 1023b31), the same object, in the way a man, a horse, a god is each in turn a living thing.

The reduction of all causal explanation to form is important to keep in mind when reading Aristotle. It gives overall coverage to his metaphysical thinking. Hamelin summed this up very trenchantly near the end of his book Le Systeme d'Aristote: "The form explains all the rest and is self-sufficient in its own right". Form is regarded as the ultimate cause, explaining all the others whether efficient, final or material, and as resting self-explanatory in its own nature. When you have reached the form you have explained the thing, and when you have come to the ultimate form you have explained all. As sight was the best of the senses because it distinguished traits so clearly, correspondingly the human way of knowing through art and science instead of just experience, is regarded in its universality as the higher type of knowledge. It is knowledge through form, thereby through cause.

With this conception of form as the ultimate in causality, Aristotle's notion of wisdom, as worked out in the opening chapters of the Metaphysics, may be understood without too much trouble in its proper historical setting. Its presentation starts, correctly enough, with the primitive Greek notion of σοφία. Although it may happen in some particular matter that a person with just experience does a thing better than a technician without experience, nevertheless in pursuance of the natural desire for knowledge people estimate the art of the trained technician as superior. It seems to them to be a higher kind of knowledge than the experience of the amateur, even though the latter happened to be more successful in a particular case. Accordingly the trained technicians are held to be 'wiser', in this still recognized sense of the Greek σοφία, than people who depend merely on their experience, in spite of the fact that on occasion these may have greater success (Metaph I.1, 981a24-7).

Aristotle does not take time out to say that the ideal is for the technician to have experience too. One naturally prefers a dentist of some experience to a student who is just finishing his course. But Aristotle's point here is solely that the technician's art is rated higher as knowledge than the amateur's experience. He asks the reason. The reason is that the technician knows the cause, while the person of mere experience does not. Wisdom is gauged according to knowledge of cause. The master-builders are therefore considered to be 'wiser' than the manual laborers, because they know the reasons, the causes, of what is being done. Knowing the reasons, the causes, the one who has the art can teach it to others. Likewise no sensation is held to be wisdom, for it does not give the reason but only the fact. On this scale the person of experience is 'wiser' than one who depends just on sensation; the technician is 'wiser' than the person of mere experience; the architect is 'wiser' than the manual workmen; those engaged in theory are 'wiser' than those who produce. The outcome is for Aristotle that wisdom par excellence is the science of the first causes and principles, according to the estimation of all. It will be the science of what is most knowable, the science pursued entirely for its own sake, the supreme science above all other sciences in virtue of knowing the causes of all (Metaph I.1-2, 981a28-982b10). It will be eminently free, and eminently teachable.[413]

What Aristotle has given in the first two chapters of the Metaphysics is a rationale of the highly elevated notion of wisdom that had come to circulate in the elite intellectual milieu of Athens in the mid-fourth century. Knowledge was the highly prized and naturally desirable goal. It was pursued to its highest instance, where it was to be found in its purity and perfection. That was theoretical contemplation, and theoretical contemplation was the true ευδαιμονία of men in its primary instance, the absolutely ultimate goal of all human striving both individual and social. Based on form, it could be regarded as the cause of its lesser instances in the arts and crafts, as well as in the moral activities that aim at an end over and above themselves.

Aristotle, however, does not commit himself to saying outright that the contemplation in which the supreme destiny of mankind consists is the primary philosophy, our science of metaphysics. He does not deny it, but he would probably have some severe qualifications if he were asked to acquiesce in that view. What he does say is that wisdom is the science of the highest causes of things, and therefore the science that meets best of all our natural desire to know. It is a σοφία, however, that remains φιλοσοφία, a love and pursuit of wisdom rather than wisdom itself. Its primary instance is theological science, or theological philosophy, that is, our metaphysics. Secondary instances are the philosophy of nature, and mathematical knowledge, which for Aristotle would cover what are called today the natural and the life sciences.[414] These three types of knowledge, metaphysics, philosophy of nature, and mathematics are for him expressly three different kinds of philosophy, three philosophies (Metaph VI.1, 1026a18). They are specifically different pursuits of wisdom, but they have their focal order towards the highest, the primary philosophy, which has as its object the highest kind of reality.

The reason why the Greek term σοφία is so sedulously avoided by Aristotle in reference to practical philosophy is not made explicit by him. Practical was contrasted with theoretical philosophy insofar as its goal was action, whereas the goal of theoretical philosophy was truth (Metaph II.1, 993b20). But besides theoretical truth there was also practical truth (EN VI.2, 1139a26-31), which practical knowledge strives to attain.[415] It is hard to see how practical science and understanding can in this context fail to be regarded as a pursuit of wisdom, a philosophy. Yet Aristotle seems to avoid deliberately the designation of it as philosophy, though he does not hesitate to call it practical science, or practical understanding. The one conjecturable reason would seem to be a tendency to avoid any connection with the notion of σοφία, a connection that the use of the term φιλοσοφία would at once imply.

On the other hand, Aristotle had no qualms in using the term φρόνησις in the opening chapters of the Metaphysics (I.1, 980b21; 2,982b24) for theoretical cognition. Apparently there was no compelling reason to restrict it to the practical order.[416] But with σοφία preempted for designating the highly exalted theoretical wisdom lauded in the Platonic world, φρόνησις could serve conveniently for a now sharply and radically distinguished practical knowledge. It bears first on variable action in the individual, and then is generalized and developed into a supreme and architectonic political science (EN,VI.7-8,1141b8-1142a9). For Plato (Polit 258D-261B) political science was sovereign and architectonic, but remained according to his use of the term a theoretical science, while practical science was restricted to knowledge for the production of corporeal things. Aristotle's sharp distinction of the practical from both the theoretical and the productive was aptly served by the reservation of the term φρόνησις to denote its sphere. Be that as it may, when the question what wisdom is for Aristotle is asked in English, the answer has to range over all three areas, the productive, the practical, and par excellence the theoretical.

[406] For instances, see LSJ, s.v. σοφία, and on the uncertain etymology Frisk, s.v. σοφός. A brief synopsis of the history of the term, and references to secondary literature, may be found in Kieran Conley, A Theology of Wisdom (Dubuque, IA: Priory Press 1963), 1-21
[407] Diogenes (8.8) gives as his source a conversation of Pythagoras with Leon, the ruler of Phlius, as found in Sosicrates of Rhodes, of the second century B.C.

[408] On the Egyptian, Hebraic and Middle Eastern notions of wisdom, see Hans Heinrich Schmidt, Wesen und Geschichte der Weisheit (Berlin. Alfred Topelmann 1966). On the Buddhist notions, see Christmas Humphreys, ed , The Wisdom of Buddhism (London: Michael Joseph 1960).

[409] A discussion of the Aristotelian meaning of φρόνησις may be found in Pierre Aubenque, La prudence chez Aristote, 1963, 155-77. Aubenque (164) notes that the opposition between σοφία and φρόνησις seems to be an invention proper to Aristotle, allowing σοφία to evoke the idea of superiority. On the background in Greek literature for the uselessness and the danger of knowledge (under either of these titles) that would surpass the ordinary, see Aubenque, 164. In the Vulgate (see Eph 1.8) sapientia is used for σοφία, prudentia for φρόνησις, without any apparent emphasis on a distinction between them.

[410] A recently published book by Wilfried Kühn, Das Prinzipienproblem in der Philosophie des Thomas von Aquin (Amsterdam: B.R. Gr ner 1982), 4-12, notes how Aquinas follows Aristotle in this radical split between theoretical and practical philosophy, rendering impossible a systematic union of the two. To this it may be replied that while the two are radically distinct in the principles from which they proceed, they both are found in the one real world. For the human mind, freedom and necessity have basically different principles, and neither can be reduced to the other. But for Aquinas (In Periherm 1.14.22) they both have the same divine cause and thereby pertain to the one universe. The one science of sacred theology can accordingly be both theoretical and practical.
[411] See Werner Wilhelm Jaeger, Paideia, III, 20-4.

[412] At Metaph I.3, 983a28, the Greek εσχατον may grammatically be either an adverb ('finally') or an adjective ('ultimate'). The understanding of it as an adverb seems required by the Aristotelian context, which is to show that to know things universally is to know them through their causes. It is only the ultimate reduction to form that gives the other causes the aspect of universality, for efficient and final causes, are individual things and matter has its being through form. A parallel problem of translation arises with τελευταΐον at 983b9, where Apostle translates adverbially ('finally') and Ross as an adjective ('the last').

[413] For the background of the theme of knowledge as teachable, see Plato, Meno 87C-99D. Corresponding to the Platonic Idea, the Aristotelian universal is the common object that makes possible the communication of knowledge. Yet with Aristotle (Metaph I 1, 980b21-5) the notion of learning, just as the notion of φρόνησις, is flexible, and is found wherever there is hearing and memory.

[414] Optics, harmonics and astronomy are regarded by Aristotle as 'the more physical branches of mathematics' (Phys II.2, 194a7-8). The mathematical basis gives the διότι, the 'reasoned fact', in these and the other mathematicized sciences.

[415] At Metaph II.1, 993b19-24, the goal of theoretical knowledge is called truth, while that of practical knowledge is action. This contrast need not exclude truth from practical knowledge. Practical knowledge, unlike theoretical knowledge just in itself, issues into action. But that action has its own kind of truth in its conformity with right reason. The designation 'philosophy of human affairs' is used for practical knowledge at EN X.9, 1181b15. There does not seem to be any sufficient reason for refusing to bring it under the notion of philosophy as 'the science of truth' (Metaph II.1, 993b20) even though it results in an effect other than itself. Yet the theoretical cast given σοφία by Aristotle seems to deter him from using the expression philosophia practica. Philosophy of nature is a 'wisdom' at Metaph IV.3, 1005b1, and all three theoretical philosophies are 'wisdoms' at III.1, 995b12 and XI.4, 1061b33.

[416] Jaeger, Aristotle, 437; 445-51, regarded this use of φρόνησις for theoretical wisdom as belonging to an earlier stage of Aristotle's work, and as Platonic in character But the use testifies to the fact that up to Aristotle's time φρόνησις could be readily understood in the sense of theoretical wisdom.
